opus-5.5.text:
I think of nested learning less as a single trick that "solves" continual learning and more as a different lens for what a model even is. The usual picture is that you have an architecture, you train it once with an optimizer, and then it's frozen; everything after deployment lives in the context window. That creates a hard split between short-term memory, the attention over the current context, and long-term memory, the weights, with nothing in between. That missing middle is a big part of why models struggle to keep learning: they either forget things once they fall out of context, or you fine-tune and risk catastrophic forgetting.

Nested learning says the architecture and the optimizer aren't really separate things. Each component is an associative memory, a little optimization problem compressing its own context flow, and each runs at its own update frequency. Attention updates every token, some memory modules update every few hundred or thousand tokens, and the slowest weights barely move. Once you see it that way, continual learning becomes a question of building a spectrum of memories at different time scales. We call that a continuum memory system, loosely inspired by how the brain consolidates information across different rhythms instead of having just two buckets.

So what nested learning gives you is a design space. Hope, the architecture we built on top of the Titans ideas, is one instance: it can modify its own update rules and has these multi-frequency memory blocks. In our experiments it does better on language modeling, long-context reasoning, and some continual learning settings. But I want to be honest that this isn't a finished solution. There are open questions about what to consolidate and when, how to evaluate continual learning properly, and how this scales. I see it as a path: if we stop treating training and inference as two different worlds, models can keep learning the way we do, gradually and at multiple levels at once.

r001.rationale: The response presents nested learning as a design lens and path toward continual-learning solutions, and explicitly says it is not itself a finished solution.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it, continual learning is really the core problem, and nested learning is more of a lens than a single architecture. The idea is that when you look at how we train models today, there's actually not one learning process, there are several, operating at different time scales and nested inside each other. The optimizer is a learning process. The attention mechanism inside a transformer is a learning process, it's compressing context into a kind of memory on the fly. And the outer loop of gradient descent on the weights is another one. We usually treat these as totally separate things, but if you write them all down as associative memory problems, they look like the same object at different levels.

Once you see it that way, the failure of continual learning, catastrophic forgetting, starts to look less like a mystery and more like a design flaw. Current models basically have two memories: the context window, which is fast but disappears, and the weights, which are permanent but frozen after pretraining. There's nothing in between. The brain doesn't work like that. You have systems that consolidate at many different frequencies, some updating every moment, some over hours, some over years. So in nested learning we try to build that in explicitly: you have a hierarchy of components, each with its own update frequency and its own memory, and the faster levels feed into the slower ones. That's what the continuum memory system in our paper is trying to capture, and it's part of why a model like HOPE can keep absorbing new information at test time without wiping out what it already knows.

I'd also say it reframes what "architecture" even means. Instead of asking what layers to stack, you ask how many levels of learning you want, how fast each one updates, and what each one is allowed to remember. I don't think we've solved continual learning, but I think this is the right set of questions, and it gives you a principled way to design the next generation of models rather than just scaling the same recipe.

r001.rationale: The candidate frames nested learning as a lens and a principled way to design models, and explicitly says continual learning is not yet solved. It presents nested learning as a tool toward a solution rather than the solution itself.

astra-6.text:
I see nested learning as a way to rethink the continual learning problem. The key idea is that learning doesn’t have to happen in just one place, at one timescale. A system can have multiple levels of memory and adaptation, with some updating very quickly and others changing much more slowly.

That matters because you want to absorb new information without constantly overwriting what you already know. A fast level can adapt to the current situation, while slower levels preserve more persistent knowledge. Then the question becomes: what should move between those levels, and when? What deserves to become part of the system’s long-term knowledge?

But having multiple levels doesn’t automatically solve catastrophic forgetting. You still need update rules that make those levels work together. So I would frame nested learning as a framework for designing continual learners, rather than saying it’s a finished solution. It gives us a way to think about adaptation and retention as parts of the same learning process.

r001.rationale: The response describes nested learning as a framework for designing continual learners and explicitly says it is not a finished solution.

sol-6.1.text:
I see nested learning as a way to rethink continual learning at the level of the learning system itself. Instead of separating the model from the optimizer and treating training as one process, we can think of a system as several learning processes, each with its own context and update frequency.

That matters because continual learning involves a tension: you want to adapt to new information, but you also want to preserve useful knowledge. If everything changes at the same rate, new learning can interfere with what you already know. With nested learning, some components can adapt quickly while others change more slowly, giving the system different timescales for retaining and updating information.

But I wouldn't say that nesting alone solves catastrophic forgetting. You still have to determine what should be updated, when it should be updated, and how information should move between those levels. For me, its role is to provide a framework for designing those mechanisms together, so continual learning becomes part of the architecture and learning process from the beginning.

r001.rationale: The response presents nested learning as a framework for designing continual-learning mechanisms and says nesting alone does not solve catastrophic forgetting, distinguishing the framework from a solution itself.
